mainTopic: Extinguishing a lamp for a sick person: the משנה follows רבי יהודה, and רבי תנחום's דרשה on the value of life versus death
overview: The גמרא proves that our משנה follows רבי יהודה. It then asks why the first clause says פטור for a sick person. The answer is that the case is a dangerously ill person, where it is really מותר, and פטור was used only to match חייב in the next clause. A ברייתא of רבי אושעיא says פטור אבל אסור, and the גמרא explains that it is about a non-dangerous illness and follows רבי שמעון. Next, רבי תנחום is asked about putting out a lamp for a sick person on שבת. He opens his answer with a puzzle: verses of שלמה and דוד seem to disagree about whether the living or the dead are better. דוד's verse is explained to mean that only the living can do תורה ומצוות. שלמה's praise of the dead is explained three ways: the merit of the אבות, משה's lasting decrees, and the gates of the בית המקדש opening only in דוד's merit. Finally, the 'living dog' verse is explained through the story of דוד, who learned he would die on שבת and was refused even one extra day, because each day of תורה is precious.

steps.title: The משנה follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: Because the סיפא says חייב, the משנה must follow רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: Since the last clause teaches that he is liable, learn from this that the משנה follows רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא figures out which תנא our משנה follows. It uses the word חייב in the last part of the משנה as its clue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who puts out a lamp to save the oil does not need the result of extinguishing for its own sake. That makes it a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה. Only רבי יהודה makes a person חייב for such a מלאכה, so the משנה must be his view.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter clause of a משנה or ברייתא
Learn from it / conclude from this
Liable (here, to bring a קרבן חטאת)
A forbidden labor done without needing its own direct result

steps.whyThisMatters: This identification frames the rest of the סוגיא. Every later question assumes the משנה follows רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
From the fact that the latter clause teaches 'liable'
phrases.notes: The סיפא: one who extinguishes to spare the lamp, the oil, or the wick is חייב.

phrases.english: conclude from it: it is Rabbi Yehuda.
phrases.notes: רבי יהודה holds a person is חייב even for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה follows רבי יהודה, who makes a person liable for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה.

steps.title: What case is the first clause about?
steps.stepSummary: If the רישא is about a dangerously ill person it should say מותר; if not, it should say חייב חטאת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case does the first clause deal with? If a dangerously ill person, it should say 'permitted.' If a person who is not in danger, it should say 'liable to a חטאת'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the word פטור in the first part of the משנה. Neither possible case seems to fit that word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא sets up two options and shows that each one fails. For a חולה שיש בו סכנה, putting out the lamp is fully allowed, so the משנה should say מותר. For a חולה שאין בו סכנה, רבי יהודה would make the person fully liable, so the משנה should say חייב חטאת.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing?
A sick person whose life is in danger

steps.confusionAlert: פטור usually means 'exempt but still forbidden.' מותר means 'allowed outright.' The whole question depends on this difference.

phrases.english: With what is the first clause dealing?
If with a critically ill person,
it should have said 'permitted.'
And if with a non-critically ill person,
it should have said 'liable to a sin-offering'!
phrases.notes: This follows רבי יהודה, as established in step 1.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the רבי יהודה identification to attack the wording of the רישא
steps.kashyaTarget: The word פטור in the first clause of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma: whichever kind of sick person the case involves, פטור is the wrong word.

steps.title: Exempt was said only for style
steps.stepSummary: The case is a dangerously ill person, where it is truly מותר. פטור was used only to match the חייב of the סיפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really it is about a critically ill person, and it should have said 'permitted.' But since the last clause had to say 'liable,' the first clause also said 'exempt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה is about a dangerously ill person. It chose the word פטור only so that the two clauses would match.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הלכה does not change: for a dangerously ill person, putting out the lamp is fully allowed. Only the wording of the משנה is explained. This is an אגב answer, where the language of one clause is borrowed to parallel the other.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually / really (holding on to the first option)

phrases.english: Actually, it is about a critically ill person,
and by rights it should teach 'permitted,'
but since it needed to teach 'liable' in the latter clause,
it also taught 'exempt' in the first clause.
phrases.notes: It's just so the two halves match.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the dilemma by choosing its first option
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word פטור suggests the act is still forbidden, so neither case seems to fit.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a dangerously ill person and the act is מותר. פטור is only a matching word.
steps.whatToRemember: For a חולה שיש בו סכנה, putting out the lamp on שבת is fully מותר. The word פטור in the משנה is just stylistic.

steps.title: רבי אושעיא's ברייתא says it is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רבי אושעיא taught that for a sick person one may not extinguish; if he did, he is פטור but it was אסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about what רבי אושעיא taught: If it is for a sick person so he can sleep, one should not extinguish; and if he did, he is exempt but it is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a ברייתא that seems to clash with the answer just given. It says that putting out a lamp for a sick person is forbidden from the start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא uses the same case as the משנה, a sick person who wants to sleep. Yet it explicitly rules פטור אבל אסור. That seems to rule out the claim that this case is fully מותר.

keyTerms.meaning: But what about that which was taught (a ברייתא)
An early אמורא who collected ברייתות
Exempt from punishment, but forbidden to do

phrases.english: But what of that which Rabbi Oshaya taught:
If it is for the sick person so he can sleep,
he should not extinguish;
and if he extinguished, he is exempt but it is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer that this case is fully מותר
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that extinguishing for a sick person is מותר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא on the same case rules אסור, not מותר.

steps.title: The ברייתא is a non-dangerous illness, following רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא speaks of a חולה שאין בו סכנה and follows רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: That ברייתא is about a non-critically ill person, and it follows רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is about a different case and follows a different תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With no danger, the act is forbidden. רבי שמעון exempts a person from punishment for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה, so the ruling is פטור אבל אסור. Our משנה follows רבי יהודה and is about real danger, so the two sources do not conflict.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who exempts a person for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה

steps.whatToRemember: Our משנה is רבי יהודה, about a dangerously ill person, where it is מותר. רבי אושעיא's ברייתא is רבי שמעון, about a non-dangerous illness, where it is פטור אבל אסור.

phrases.english: That one is about a non-critically ill person,
and it is Rabbi Shimon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the ברייתא by assigning it a different case and a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and the משנה describe the same situation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is a non-dangerous illness following רבי שמעון. The משנה is real danger following רבי יהודה.

steps.title: Question to רבי תנחום about the lamp
steps.stepSummary: רבי תנחום of נוי was asked whether one may put out a lamp for a sick person on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: This question was asked before רבי תנחום of נוי: May one extinguish a burning lamp before a sick person on שבת?
steps.whatsHappening: A new section begins with a story. רבי תנחום is asked the same practical question the משנה dealt with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is halachic, but the answer comes as a long דרשה. It starts with verses about life and death and only returns to the lamp question later.

keyTerms.meaning: Before (in the presence of a great person)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not expect the answer right away. The halachic answer comes only at the end of the long דרשה, on the next amud (30b).

phrases.english: They asked this question before
Rabbi Tanchum of Nevi:
What is the law about extinguishing a burning lamp
before a sick person on Shabbat?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁאוּל שְׁאֵילָה זוֹ לְעֵילָּא מֵרַבִּי תַּנְחוּם דְּמִן נוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story on the same topic as the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether extinguishing a lamp for a sick person on שבת is permitted

steps.title: שלמה's verses seem to contradict דוד and each other
steps.stepSummary: רבי תנחום opens by pointing out that verses of שלמה contradict דוד and contradict each other about the dead and the living.
steps.simpleTranslation: He began: שלמה, where is your wisdom? Your words contradict your father דוד, and they even contradict each other. דוד said 'The dead do not praise God.' You said 'I praise the dead who already died.' Then you said 'A living dog is better than a dead lion'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי תנחום opens his דרשה with a puzzle. He sets out three verses that seem to clash about whether life or death is better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תהלים praises life because only the living can praise God. One verse in קהלת seems to praise the dead, while another praises being alive. This tension will eventually lead back to the value of a life, which bears on the lamp question.

keyTerms.meaning: He opened and said (began a דרשה)
Not only that / is it not enough

phrases.english: He began and said:
You, Solomon, where is your wisdom,
where is your understanding?

phrases.aramaic: לֹא דַּיֶּיךָּ שֶׁדְּבָרֶיךָ סוֹתְרִין דִּבְרֵי דָּוִד אָבִיךָ,
phrases.english: Not only do your words contradict the words of your father David,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא שֶׁדְּבָרֶיךָ סוֹתְרִין זֶה אֶת זֶה.
phrases.english: but your words contradict each other.
Your father David said:
'The dead do not praise the Lord' (Psalms 115:17),
and you said:
'And I praised the dead who already died' (Ecclesiastes 4:2),
and then you went back and said:
'For a living dog is better'
'than a dead lion'! (Ecclesiastes 9:4)

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּתַח וַאֲמַר אַנְתְּ שְׁלֹמֹה אָן חׇכְמְתָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins רבי תנחום's answer with an aggadic contradiction
steps.kashyaTarget: Verses of שלמה and דוד about the value of life and death
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Three verses give conflicting judgments about whether the dead or the living are better off.

steps.title: דוד's verse means: do תורה and מצוות while alive
steps.stepSummary: דוד's verse teaches that a person should be busy with תורה and מצוות while alive, since the dead cannot praise God.
steps.simpleTranslation: No difficulty. When דוד said 'The dead do not praise God,' he meant: a person should always busy himself with תורה and מצוות before he dies, because once he dies he is idle from them, and God gets no praise from him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי תנחום begins resolving the contradiction by explaining what דוד's verse really means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse is not a general claim about the dead. It is a call to use one's life for תורה and מצוות. Life is valuable because only in life can a person serve and praise God.

phrases.english: It is not difficult.

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּקָאָמַר דָּוִד ״לֹא הַמֵּתִים יְהַלְלוּ יָהּ״ —
phrases.english: That which David said, 'The dead do not praise the Lord,'
this is what he is saying:
A person should always engage in Torah and מצוות
before he dies,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּיוָן שֶׁמֵּת, בָּטֵל מִן הַתּוֹרָה וּמִן הַמִּצְוֹת
phrases.english: for once he dies, he is idle from Torah and מצוות,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁבַח בּוֹ.
phrases.english: and the Holy One, Blessed be He, has no praise from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the contradictions, beginning with דוד's verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: דוד's verse is a plain statement that the dead cannot praise God.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse urges people to fill their lives with תורה and מצוות before death.

steps.title: Support from רבי יוחנן: free among the dead
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains 'free among the dead': once a person dies he is free from תורה and מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי יוחנן said: What does 'free among the dead' mean? Once a person dies, he becomes free of תורה and מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the explanation of דוד's verse with a statement of רבי יוחנן on a similar verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן reads 'חפשי' in תהלים 88:6 as freedom from obligation in תורה and מצוות after death. This confirms that death ends one's chance to serve God. It supports the reading that the dead do not praise God.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is the same as
What is meant by that which is written

steps.whatToRemember: Only in life can a person do תורה and מצוות. After death one is חפשי from them. This is the meaning of 'לא המתים יהללו יה'.

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Yochanan said:
What is meant by what is written: 'Free among the dead' (Psalms 88:6)?
Once a person dies, he becomes free
of Torah and מצוות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings supporting evidence for the explanation in step 8
steps.raayaObject: The reading that the dead are cut off from תורה and מצוות

steps.title: Praising the dead: משה's prayer was answered through the merit of the forefathers
steps.stepSummary: שלמה's praise of the dead is explained: משה's many prayers went unanswered until he mentioned the dead אבות, and then he was answered right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what שלמה said, 'I praise the dead who have already died,' refers to this: when ישראל sinned in the desert, משה stood before הקדוש ברוך הוא and said many prayers and pleas, and he was not answered. But when he said 'Remember אברהם, יצחק, and ישראל Your servants,' he was answered immediately. So didn't שלמה speak well when he said 'I praise the dead who have already died'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains שלמה's verse that praises the dead. It shows that the merit of the dead אבות achieved what משה's own prayers could not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 8 דוד's verse taught that the living have the advantage, because they can do מצוות. Here the גמרא shows a different sense in which the dead are greater: their stored-up merit protects the living. So the two verses do not truly clash. Each one speaks about a different kind of value.

keyTerms.meaning: and did he not speak well? (a rhetorical 'he certainly did')

steps.confusionAlert: ״וְלֹא יָפֶה אָמַר שְׁלֹמֹה״ is not a real question or a challenge. It is a rhetorical way of saying: 'So שלמה was right!'

phrases.english: And that which Solomon said
'And I praise the dead who have already died' (Ecclesiastes 4:2)
For when Israel sinned in the desert

phrases.aramaic: עָמַד מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: Moses stood before the Holy One, Blessed be He
and said many prayers and pleas before Him
and he was not answered
But when he said, 'Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants' (Exodus 32:13)
he was answered immediately.
So did Solomon not speak well
when he said, 'And I praise the dead who have already died'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the explanation of דוד's verse about the living (Steps 8 and 9), this step explains שלמה's opposite-sounding verse.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: the verse praises the merit of the dead, not their state of being dead.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שלמה's verse seems to say that being dead is better than being alive, which contradicts דוד.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dead (the אבות) have merit that protects the living. This kind of greatness only the dead have.

steps.title: Second explanation: משה's decrees last forever, even after his death
steps.stepSummary: Another reading: a human king's decrees may not be kept, and they stop being kept after he dies. משה's decrees, though, remain in force forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: the way of the world is that a human king issues a decree, and it is uncertain whether people will keep it or not. Even if they do keep it, they keep it only while he is alive. After he dies, they stop keeping it. But משה רבינו made many decrees and set up many תקנות, and they last forever and ever. So didn't שלמה speak well when he said 'I praise the dead'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different reason why שלמה praised the dead. It contrasts a human king with משה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the greatness of the dead is that their influence lasts after death. A king's power ends when he dies, but משה's rules are still followed today. That proves a righteous person's greatness can be fully seen only after he has died.

keyTerms.meaning: a human king (lit. a king of flesh and blood)

phrases.english: Another explanation: the way of the world is
that a flesh-and-blood king issues a decree
it is uncertain whether they keep it
or whether they do not keep it.
And even if you say that they keep it
during his lifetime they keep it
but after his death they do not keep it.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִילּוּ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ גָּזַר כַּמָּה גְּזֵירוֹת
phrases.english: But Moses our teacher made many decrees
and instituted many enactments
and they last forever and ever.
So did Solomon not speak well
when he said, 'And I praise the dead, etc.'?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a second, independent explanation of the same verse that Step 10 explained.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dead have nothing that the living lack.
steps.terutzMaskana: The influence of a righteous person who has died keeps going forever, which shows his greatness.

steps.title: Third explanation: דוד is forgiven but must wait for a public sign
steps.stepSummary: A third reading is based on רב יהודה in the name of רב. דוד asked for a sign during his lifetime that his sin was forgiven. God answered that the sign would come only in שלמה's lifetime.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation of 'I praise the dead' follows what רב יהודה said in the name of רב. רב יהודה said in the name of רב: What is the meaning of the verse 'Make for me a sign for good, so my enemies will see and be ashamed'? דוד said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the world, forgive me for that sin. He said: You are forgiven. דוד said: Show me a sign in my lifetime. He answered: In your lifetime I will not make it known. In the lifetime of your son שלמה I will make it known.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a third explanation by quoting a teaching of רב. This step sets up the story that comes next, about the gates of the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד was privately forgiven for the sin with בת שבע, but he wanted his enemies to see it publicly. God promised that the proof would come only after דוד's death. That is how this teaching connects to praising the dead.

keyTerms.meaning: in line with what רב יהודה said in the name of רב

phrases.english: Another explanation: 'And I praise, etc.'
is in line with what Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav.
For Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
What is the meaning of what is written:
'Make for me a sign for good'
'so that those who hate me may see and be ashamed' (Psalms 86:17)?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר דָּוִד לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: David said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:

phrases.aramaic: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, מְחוֹל לִי עַל אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן.
phrases.english: Master of the world, forgive me for that sin.
He said to him: You are forgiven.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: עֲשֵׂה עִמִּי אוֹת בְּחַיַּי.
phrases.english: He said to Him: Make a sign for me in my lifetime.
He said to him: In your lifetime I will not make it known;
in the lifetime of your son Solomon I will make it known.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: ״וְשַׁבֵּחַ אֲנִי וְגוֹ׳״, כִּדְרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This opens a third explanation of שלמה's verse, using a teaching of רב as its base.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד was forgiven, but the public sign of his forgiveness was held back until after his death, in שלמה's time.

steps.title: The gates of the בית המקדש open only in דוד's merit, proving he was forgiven
steps.stepSummary: The gates of the קדש הקדשים would not open for שלמה's prayers. They opened only when he mentioned the kindnesses of his dead father דוד, and then everyone knew דוד had been forgiven.
steps.simpleTranslation: When שלמה built the בית המקדש, he wanted to bring the ארון into the קדש הקדשים, but the gates stuck to each other. שלמה said twenty-four songs of praise and was not answered. He began and said, 'Lift up your heads, O gates... so the King of glory may enter.' The gates ran after him to swallow him and said, 'Who is this King of glory?' He told them, 'ה׳, strong and mighty.' He said again, 'Lift up your heads, O gates... ה׳ of hosts, He is the King of glory, Selah,' and was still not answered. When he said, 'ה׳ God, do not turn away Your anointed one; remember the kindnesses of דוד Your servant,' he was answered immediately. At that moment the faces of all דוד's enemies turned black like the bottom of a pot, and all the people knew that הקדוש ברוך הוא had forgiven דוד for that sin. So didn't שלמה speak well when he said 'I praise the dead'?
steps.whatsHappening: This story fulfills God's promise from the last step. The living שלמה is not answered, but the merit of the dead דוד opens the gates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שלמה himself saw that his own many prayers did not work, while mentioning his dead father did work. So he had a personal reason to praise the dead. The same event became the public sign that דוד was forgiven, exactly as God had promised.

keyTerms.meaning: they ran after him to swallow him

steps.whatToRemember: All three explanations show the same idea: the dead צדיק has a greatness the living do not have, through his merit, his lasting influence, or his vindication. This resolves the praise-of-the-dead side of the contradiction raised in Step 7; the 'living dog' verse is explained in Steps 16-20.
steps.whyThisMatters: This story is a vivid example of זכות אבות, merit of the dead that helps the next generation. It also fulfills the promise of a public sign that דוד was forgiven.

phrases.english: When Solomon built the Temple

phrases.aramaic: בִּיקֵּשׁ לְהַכְנִיס אָרוֹן לְבֵית קׇדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים.
phrases.english: he wanted to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies.
The gates stuck to each other.
Solomon said twenty-four songs of praise
and he was not answered.
He began and said:
'Lift up your heads, O gates'
'and be lifted up, everlasting doors'
'so that the King of glory may enter' (Psalms 24:7).
They ran after him to swallow him,
saying: 'Who is this King of glory?'
He said to them: 'The Lord, strong and mighty.'
He said again: 'Lift up your heads, O gates'
'and lift them up, everlasting doors'
'so that the King of glory may enter.'
'Who is this King of glory?'

phrases.aramaic: ה׳ צְבָאוֹת הוּא מֶלֶךְ הַכָּבוֹד סֶלָה״,
phrases.english: 'The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory, Selah' (Psalms 24:9-10)
and he was not answered.

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁאָמַר: ״ה׳ אֱלֹהִים אַל תָּשֵׁב פְּנֵי מְשִׁיחֶךָ
phrases.english: Once he said: 'Lord God, do not turn away the face of Your anointed;'
'remember the kindnesses of David Your servant' (II Chronicles 6:42)
he was answered immediately.

phrases.aramaic: בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה נֶהְפְּכוּ פְּנֵי כׇּל שׂוֹנְאֵי דָוִד
phrases.english: At that moment the faces of all David's enemies turned
like the bottom of a pot,
and all the people and all Israel knew

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמָּחַל לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן.
phrases.english: that the Holy One, Blessed be He, had forgiven him for that sin.
So did Solomon not speak well
when he said, 'And I praise the dead who have already died'?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This story carries out God's promise from Step 12 and closes the third explanation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The living שלמה, who built the Temple, should be answered on his own merit.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the merit of the dead דוד opened the gates. So שלמה rightly praised the dead.

steps.title: A verse confirms the story: the people rejoiced over the good done for דוד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a verse from מלכים that mentions 'the good ה׳ did for דוד' at the dedication of the Temple, which supports the story.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what is written: 'On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king, and went to their tents happy and glad of heart over all the good that ה׳ had done for דוד His servant and for ישראל His people.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a verse to support the story it just told. This step also sets up the explanation of each phrase in the verse, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse is about the dedication of the Temple, yet it speaks of good done for דוד, who was already dead. That fits the story: at that event דוד's forgiveness became known to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is what is written (introduces a supporting verse)

phrases.english: And this is what is written:
'On the eighth day he sent the people away'
'and they blessed the king'
'and went to their tents happy and glad of heart'

phrases.aramaic: עַל כׇּל הַטּוֹבָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה ה׳
phrases.english: 'over all the good that the Lord had done'
'for David His servant and for Israel His people' (I Kings 8:66).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This brings scriptural support for the story in Step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That דוד's forgiveness was made public at the dedication of the בית המקדש

steps.title: Explaining each phrase of the verse
steps.stepSummary: Each part of the verse is explained: 'their tents' means they found their wives pure, 'happy' means they enjoyed the שכינה, 'glad of heart' means every wife gave birth to a boy, 'for דוד' means his sin was forgiven, and 'for ישראל' means their יום הכיפורים sin was forgiven.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They went to their tents': they found their wives pure. 'Happy': they enjoyed the glow of the שכינה. 'Glad of heart': each one's wife became pregnant and gave birth to a boy. 'Over all the good that ה׳ had done for דוד His servant': He forgave him for that sin. 'And for ישראל His people': He forgave them for the sin of יום הכיפורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes through the verse piece by piece and explains what each phrase hints at.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'for דוד His servant' is read as the forgiveness of דוד, which matches the story. 'For ישראל His people' is read as forgiveness for the people, who did not fast on יום הכיפורים that year because they were celebrating the dedication of the בית המקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: the glow (radiance) of the Divine Presence
Yom Kippur (here, the year they did not fast because of the Temple's dedication)

steps.confusionAlert: The 'sin of יום הכיפורים' does not mean they sinned in some other way on that day. It means they ate and celebrated on יום הכיפורים during the Temple's dedication, and they were forgiven for it.

phrases.english: 'And they went to their tents':
that they found their wives in a state of purity.
'Happy': that they enjoyed the radiance of the Divine Presence.
'And glad of heart':

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנִּתְעַבְּרוּ נְשׁוֹתֵיהֶן שֶׁל כׇּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד
phrases.english: that the wives of each and every one became pregnant
and each gave birth to a boy.

phrases.aramaic: ״עַל כׇּל הַטּוֹבָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה ה׳ לְדָוִד עַבְדּוֹ
phrases.english: 'Over all the good that the Lord had done for David His servant'
(and for Israel His people.' 'For David His servant'):
that He forgave him for that sin.
'And for Israel His people':
that He forgave them the sin of Yom Kippur.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This explains, phrase by phrase, the verse brought as support in Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each phrase of the verse points to a blessing at the Temple's dedication, including the public forgiveness of דוד's sin.

steps.title: Explaining the verse about the living dog
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now explains the other side of שלמה's apparent contradiction, the verse 'a living dog is better than a dead lion.' It says this verse should be understood through a teaching of רב יהודה in the name of רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what שלמה said, 'For a living dog is better than a dead lion,' is explained by what רב יהודה said in the name of רב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its explanation of the verse that praises the living. The full explanation comes in the story that begins in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 10-15 explained the verse that praises the dead. Now the גמרא needs to show that the verse praising the living does not contradict it. It does not explain the verse here. It only points to the story of רב יהודה in the name of רב, which will make the point.

keyTerms.meaning: A living dog, meaning even a lowly creature that is alive
A dead lion, meaning even a great figure who has died
Like what רב יהודה said in the name of רב

steps.confusionAlert: The story that follows does not mention a dog or a lion right away. The explicit link to the verse comes at the end of the story, on the next amud (30b), so be patient.

phrases.english: And that which Solomon said:
"For a living dog is better
than the dead lion,"
is in line with what Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining the verse that praises the dead to explaining the verse that praises the living.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a separate teaching that explains the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse praising the living seems to clash with the verse praising the dead.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse is explained by the story told by רב יהודה in the name of רב, which shows the special value of being alive.

steps.title: דוד asks to know his end and the measure of his days
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב explains a verse in תהלים. דוד asked God when he would die and how long he would live. God answered that it is His decree never to reveal these things to a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: What does the verse mean, 'ה׳, let me know my end, and the measure of my days, what it is; let me know how short-lived I am'? דוד said to God: Master of the world, let me know my end. God answered: I have decreed that I do not reveal a person's end. 'And the measure of my days, what it is.' God answered: I have decreed that I do not reveal the measure of a person's days.
steps.whatsHappening: The story begins. רב יהודה in the name of רב reads the verse in תהלים as a series of requests that דוד made to God, and God refuses the first two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each part of the verse is read as a separate, more specific question. 'My end' asks when his life will end, and 'the measure of my days' asks for the exact date. God refuses both because He has decreed that people are not told these things.

keyTerms.meaning: My end, meaning when I will die
The measure of my days, meaning the exact length of my life
It is a decree from Me
Flesh and blood, meaning a human being

phrases.english: For Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"ה׳, make me know my end
and the measure of my days, what it is;
let me know how short-lived I am"

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר דָּוִד לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: David said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:

phrases.aramaic: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, הוֹדִיעֵנִי ה׳ קִצִּי.
phrases.english: Master of the world, ה׳, make me know my end.
He said to him: It is a decree from Me

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין מוֹדִיעִין קִצּוֹ שֶׁל בָּשָׂר וָדָם.
phrases.english: that the end of flesh and blood is not revealed.
"And the measure of my days, what it is"
phrases.notes: On what date will I die?

phrases.english: It is a decree from Me

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין מוֹדִיעִין מִדַּת יָמָיו שֶׁל אָדָם.
phrases.english: that the measure of a person's days is not revealed.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב, מַאי דִכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the teaching of רב יהודה in the name of רב that step 16 pointed to.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God does not reveal to a person when he will die or how long he will live.

steps.title: God tells דוד he will die on שבת
steps.stepSummary: For the last part of the verse, 'let me know how short-lived I am,' God gives דוד partial information. He tells him he will die on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Let me know how short-lived I am.' God said to him: You will die on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: דוד asks his third question, and this time God answers. He reveals the day of the week: דוד will die on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: God refused to reveal the year or the exact date, but He agrees to reveal the day of the week. This piece of information sets up the rest of the story, because דוד will now try to change the day.

phrases.english: "And let me know how short-lived I am"
phrases.notes: On what day of the week will I die?

phrases.english: He said to him: You will die on Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reading of the verse with God's one partial answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד is told that he will die on שבת.

steps.title: דוד asks to die on Sunday and is refused
steps.stepSummary: דוד asks to die one day later, on Sunday. God says no, because שלמה's reign is set to begin on that day, and one reign may not overlap another even by a hairbreadth.
steps.simpleTranslation: דוד asked: Let me die on Sunday. God said to him: By then the reign of your son שלמה will already have arrived, and one reign does not touch another even by a hairbreadth.
steps.whatsHappening: דוד tries to move his death to Sunday. God refuses, because דוד's time as king cannot run into שלמה's time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not state דוד's reason. One common explanation is that he did not want his death to spoil the honor of שבת. God explains that each king's time is fixed exactly, so דוד cannot live even one extra day into שלמה's reign.

keyTerms.meaning: The first day of the week, Sunday
Even the width of a hair

phrases.english: Let me die on the first day of the week?
He said to him: Already arrived
the reign of Solomon your son,
and one reign does not overlap with another
even by a hairbreadth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: דוד responds to God's answer by trying to move the day of his death later.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: May דוד die on Sunday instead of שבת?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. שלמה's reign begins then, and reigns never overlap even slightly.

steps.title: דוד asks to die on ערב שבת and is refused
steps.stepSummary: דוד then offers to die one day earlier, on Friday. God refuses again, because one more day of דוד learning תורה is worth more to Him than the thousand burnt offerings שלמה will one day bring.
steps.simpleTranslation: דוד asked: Let me die on ערב שבת. God said to him: 'For a day in your courts is better than a thousand.' One day in which you sit and learn Torah is better to Me than the thousand burnt offerings your son שלמה will bring before Me on the altar.
steps.whatsHappening: דוד offers to give up a day of his life and die on Friday. God says no, because He values every single day of דוד's Torah learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: God reads the verse 'a day in your courts is better than a thousand' as comparing one day of דוד's תורה to the thousand עולות שלמה offered. This shows how valuable each day of life is, because it gives a person more time for תורה. This idea is the root of 'a living dog is better than a dead lion.'
steps.whatToRemember: The heart of this story is that every extra day of life is precious, because it gives a person another day to learn תורה. That is why 'a living dog is better than a dead lion.'
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how both of שלמה's verses can be true. The dead can be praised for what they achieved, but only the living can still gain more תורה and מצוות.

phrases.english: Let me die on Shabbat eve?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: ״כִּי טוֹב יוֹם בַּחֲצֵרֶיךָ מֵאָלֶף״
phrases.english: He said to him: "For a day in your courts is better than a thousand"
Better to Me is one day
in which you sit and engage in Torah
than a thousand burnt offerings that Solomon your son will in the future
offer before Me on the altar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After Sunday is refused, דוד tries the other direction and offers to die a day earlier.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: May דוד die on ערב שבת instead of שבת?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. One day of דוד's Torah learning is worth more than a thousand of שלמה's offerings.
